summary.en: The alphabet and the tricky sounds, ijekavian, Bosnian vs Croatian words, and noun gender and plural.
summary.bs: Abeceda i teški glasovi, ijekavica, bosanske i hrvatske riječi, te rod i množina imenica.

en.one: Bosnian and Croatian use the Latin alphabet of 30 letters, and every letter is always pronounced the same way.
en.explain: 'Write as you speak, read as you write' – there are no silent letters. Special letters: č, ć, dž, đ, š, ž and the pairs lj and nj, which count as single letters. 'j' sounds like English y (ja = 'ya'), 'c' is always 'ts' (centar), 'r' is rolled and can even be a vowel (prst – finger, Trst – Trieste). Stress is never on the last syllable.
en.example: šuma (forest, 'shoo-ma'), žaba (frog, like the s in 'pleasure'), ljubav (love, 'lyoo-bav'), njegov (his, 'nyeh-gov').
en.why: Once you know the letter sounds, you can read any word aloud correctly, even if you don't know what it means.
en.mixup: Bosnian also uses Cyrillic officially, but Latin is standard in daily life. Croatian uses only Latin.

en.one: Four letters that confuse learners: č and ć (both like 'ch'), dž and đ (both like 'j').
en.explain: č is hard, with the tongue pulled back: like 'ch' in 'church' (čaj – tea). ć is soft, with the tongue forward, closer to 'tj' (kuća – house). dž is hard, like 'j' in 'jungle' (džep – pocket). đ is soft (đak – pupil, rođendan – birthday). Many speakers in Bosnia blur them, but in writing they must be right.
en.example: čovjek (man), noć (night), sreća (luck / happiness), džamija (mosque), međunarodni (international).
en.why: They change meaning: 'kuća' is house, but a 'kuča' doesn't exist. Spelling mistakes here are very visible.
en.mixup: Verb infinitives ending in -ći always use ć: ići, moći, doći, reći.

en.one: Bosnian and Croatian are 'ijekavian': an old vowel is pronounced 'ije' (long) or 'je' (short). Serbian mostly uses 'e' (ekavian).
en.explain: Long: mlijeko (milk), lijep (beautiful), rijeka (river), vrijeme (time / weather). Short: mjesto (place), djeca (children), vjera (faith), sjesti (sit down). In some words it becomes 'i' or 'e': htio (wanted), vidjeti → vidio.
en.example: Bosnian/Croatian 'lijepo mlijeko' vs. Serbian 'lepo mleko'. Both are understood everywhere in the region.
en.why: Using ijekavian forms is part of writing correct Bosnian and Croatian.
en.mixup: Not every 'e' becomes 'ije': 'selo' (village) and 'zemlja' (land) have a normal e. Learn ijekavian words as they come.

en.one: Bosnian and Croatian share the same grammar. They differ in some words and a few habits. In this program the Croatian word is shown in brackets: hljeb (kruh).
en.explain: Common word pairs: hljeb (kruh) – bread, sedmica (tjedan) – week, hiljada (tisuća) – thousand, voz (vlak) – train, historija (povijest) – history, porodica (obitelj) – family, kafa (kava) – coffee, šta (što) – what, ko (tko) – who, tačka (točka) – full stop, juli (srpanj) – July. Grammar habits: Bosnian often says 'da li' and 'trebam da idem', Croatian prefers 'je li' and 'trebam ići'.
en.example: Bosnian: 'Šta radiš ove sedmice?' Croatian: 'Što radiš ovaj tjedan?' Both mean 'What are you doing this week?'
en.why: You'll be understood everywhere with either form. Knowing both helps you read Croatian media and talk with people from both countries.
en.mixup: Croatian also uses its own month names (siječanj, veljača…), while Bosnian uses januar, februar… Don't mix them in one text.

en.one: Every noun has a gender: muški (masculine), ženski (feminine) or srednji (neuter). Unlike German, you can usually see it from the ending.
en.explain: Masculine: ends in a consonant (grad, sto (stol), prozor). Feminine: ends in -a (kuća, žena, knjiga), plus some in a consonant (noć, ljubav, stvar). Neuter: ends in -o or -e (selo, more, dijete, srce). Male people ending in -a are still masculine in meaning: tata, sudija (sudac).
en.example: 'nov grad', 'nova kuća', 'novo selo'. The adjective shows the gender too.
en.why: Gender decides adjective endings, pronouns and the past tense (radio / radila / radilo).
en.mixup: Feminine nouns ending in a consonant are a trap: 'ta noć' (that night), not 'taj noć'.

en.one: The plural (množina) depends on the gender of the noun.
en.explain: Masculine: add -i, and short one-syllable nouns often add -ovi/-evi: student → studenti, grad → gradovi, muž → muževi. Feminine in -a: change to -e: žena → žene, kuća → kuće. Neuter: -o/-e becomes -a: selo → sela, more → mora. Irregular: čovjek → ljudi (people), dijete → djeca (children), oko → oči (eyes), uho → uši (ears).
en.example: 'jedan prozor, dva prozora, mnogo prozora' – the ending also changes after numbers (topic 8).
en.why: You'll need plural forms all the time, and the irregular ones are some of the most common words.
en.mixup: 'Djeca' is a special case: its adjectives look feminine singular ('mala djeca'), but the verb is plural ('Djeca su se igrala'). A famous exception.
